title: Chapter 7: De Rham Theory
notes: Open by naming the theme of the chapter. Differential forms are already analytic objects, but de Rham theory asks which closed forms have global potentials and which ones remember topology. Use the roadmap to prepare students for the lecture rhythm: one obstruction, then bookkeeping machines, then homotopy invariance, then computations.

title: Closed Need Not Mean Exact
notes: Pause on the distinction because it drives every later construction. Closed is a local differential condition, while exact is the existence of a global primitive. Students should hear that exact implies closed for a formal reason, namely d squared is zero, but the reverse can fail because a global loop detects incompatible local primitives.

title: Angular Period Obstruction
notes: Use the punctured plane as the chapter's first concrete witness. The displayed form is closed away from the origin, so locally it passes the exterior derivative test. The period around the unit circle is two pi, and that number rules out exactness because integrals of exact one-forms over closed loops are zero.

title: Definition Of De Rham Cohomology
notes: Present the quotient slowly and tie every symbol to the previous slide. Z k is the closed part, B k is the exact part, and d squared equal to zero ensures B k sits inside Z k. The quotient forgets changes by global potentials and keeps precisely the period data that exact forms cannot carry.

title: First Calculations
notes: Use these examples to calibrate the invariant before introducing heavier machinery. Degree zero counts connected components because a closed function is locally constant. On the real line every closed one-form has a global primitive, while the circle retains one independent period. The dimension bound reminds students that the complex stops at the manifold dimension.

title: Functoriality And Ring Structure
notes: Emphasize that pullback is the natural operation on forms, so cohomology runs opposite to smooth maps. The key calculation is d commuting with pullback, which preserves both closed and exact forms. Then add the second payoff: wedge product survives the quotient and turns de Rham cohomology into a graded ring with signs.

title: Exactness Bookkeeping
notes: Before using exact sequences, make the phrase exact at a node completely concrete. The image of one map must be the entire kernel of the next map. The cohomology formula is exactly the measure of failure of exactness: closed things in the kernel modulo exact things coming from the previous image.

title: Cochain Complexes And Zig-Zags
notes: Explain the connecting map as a construction rather than as a symbol. Start with a closed class in C, lift it to B, apply the differential, and exactness forces the result to come from A in the next degree. The zig-zag proof is the algebraic engine later used for Mayer-Vietoris.

title: Mayer-Vietoris Machine
notes: Frame Mayer-Vietoris as the chapter's main computation machine. Forms restrict to U and V, and the difference of the two restrictions on the overlap measures whether local data agree. The partition-of-unity move splits overlap data into pieces that extend over U and V, which is the practical reason the short complex is exact. The resulting long exact sequence converts cover information into cohomology.

title: Circle By Mayer-Vietoris
notes: Work through the circle as a dimension argument. The two covering arcs are contractible, but their intersection has two components. In the long exact sequence this extra component count cannot be absorbed by the connected circle and its two arc constants, so one dimension remains in H one. That remaining dimension is the period class from the angular form.

title: Euler Characteristic
notes: Introduce Euler characteristic as a compact shadow of the full cohomology calculation. It is not as informative as the ring or the individual groups, but the alternating sum is easy to track through exact sequences. The table also previews the surface result: a genus g surface has middle Betti number two g and Euler characteristic two minus two g.

title: Homotopy And Retraction
notes: This is the geometric reason cohomology deserves to be called topological. The punctured plane looks two-dimensional and noncompact, but radial deformation keeps its circle of directions. The angular class is unchanged under the retraction, so the computation reduces to the circle without losing the period obstruction.

title: Homotopy Axiom And Poincare Lemma
notes: Connect two ideas that can otherwise feel separate. The Poincare lemma says de Rham cohomology vanishes locally in positive degree, so nonzero classes must be global obstructions. The homotopy axiom says smooth deformation does not alter those classes. Together, they justify computing with simpler homotopy models while still respecting local calculus.

title: Torus Computation
notes: Use the torus to make the ring structure tangible. There are two independent one-forms, alpha and beta, one for each circle direction. Their wedge product is the top area class, and swapping them changes the sign. This is the first computation where the product structure says more than the list of dimensions.

title: Surface Genus And Degree
notes: Pull the computations into recognizable invariants. For a closed oriented surface of genus g, the first Betti number is two g, one pair for each handle, and the Euler characteristic is two minus two g. Then explain the degree-style statement: on top cohomology, pullback by a degree d map multiplies the orientation generator by d.

title: Cochain Homotopy Proof Mechanism
notes: Close with the proof idea rather than a long formal proof. The endpoint pullbacks from M times the interval differ by an exact cochain-level expression, d K plus K d, where K integrates the contraction of the form with the interval vector field partial t from zero to one. Once a closed form is passed to cohomology, that difference disappears. The whole homotopy axiom is therefore the fundamental theorem of calculus written in the language of forms.
